entities.summary:
Aeschines was a prominent Greek statesman and orator who played a significant role in the development of Athenian democracy.

As a member of the prominent Athenian family known as the Aeschines, he rose to prominence through his exceptional eloquence and mastery of rhetoric. By 350 BCE, he had become one of the ten most influential Attic orators, rivaled only by figures such as Demosthenes.

Aeschines' most notable achievement was his service as a prosecutor in several high-profile cases against rival politicians, including the infamous trial of Timocles.

His involvement with Timocles led to Aeschines' own downfall when he was eventually convicted and exiled. Despite this, his legacy continued to influence Athenian politics for generations.

Aeschines' impact on world history can be seen in the enduring power of Athenian democracy and the development of Western legal precedents.

A self-made man of modest origins (his father ran a grammar school and his mother performed mystery rites), Aeschines rose through his extraordinary talent for improvised speech and his physical presence — he was a trained actor before entering politics, and his theatrical skills gave him a style of oratory that was the antithesis of Demosthenes' laboured, intensely prepared speeches. The personal and political rivalry between Aeschines and Demosthenes, conducted through two decades of lawsuits, counter-accusations, and political manoeuvres, is one of the most fully documented political conflicts of the ancient world.

The climactic confrontation came in 330 BCE: Aeschines prosecuted the prominent Athenian Ctesiphon for proposing to award Demosthenes a golden crown for his service to Athens. This produced Demosthenes' masterpiece 'On the Crown' — the greatest speech of ancient oratory — and Aeschines' own 'Against Ctesiphon'. Aeschines lost so decisively (failing to reach even one-fifth of the jury's votes) that he was fined and forced into exile in Rhodes, where he taught rhetoric.
